title: Modern Nostr Index Card-based Knowledge Engineering
description: Some concepts explored related to Knowledge Engineering, Nostr, Large Language Models, Complexity, and more.

methods.name: Index cards as hashed Nostr notes (JSON to SHA256 ID)
methods.description: The notes sketch each index card as a JSON object (username, text, etc.) hashed into a 32-byte SHA256 identifier, with edges defined between card IDs.
methods.evidence: has JSON: Username, Text, etc — then hashes into 32 bytes, SHA256.

methods.name: LLM semantic embeddings attached to index cards
methods.description: Proposes using language-model embeddings, translations and summaries so cards act as semantic bridges between texts.
methods.evidence: Using semantic embeddings from LLM (and translations, summaries) to use index cards as contextual/semantic bridges.

methods.name: Path analysis over composed index-card graphs
methods.description: Proposes analyzing paths through card graphs for trivial features (overall length) and subtler ones (e.g. which proportion of links are novel reports).
methods.evidence: Paths can be analyzed for trivial features (e.g. overall length) or various subtle things (e.g. which proportion of links are novel reports).

key_findings: The notes propose linking papers not only by citation edges but by syntactic bridges (keyword cards) and semantic bridges (embeddings).
The notes argue auto-generated flashcards pose less of an information-overload risk than auto-generated papers, since unused cards are simply ignored and useful ones composed.
The notes suggest review papers could follow the most popular paths through the card graph and novelty search the least traversed ones.
key_findings_evidence: Moving between the papers, not just with a citation edge. Could be with a Syntax side (e.g. bridging via a keyword Index Cards) and with a Semantic side (via the embeddings).
Don’t need to worry about auto-generated content with Flashcards. Because useless ones are simply not used. Useful ones are composed together
Review paper — most popular paths. • Novelty search — least traversed paths.
